author: Herwig, Holger H.
title: The Marne, 1914: The Opening of World War I and the Battle That Changed the World
notes: The standard modern operational narrative of the 1914 campaign in the West; uses German, French and British archives. Primary source for army movements, dates and strengths.

author: Tuchman, Barbara W.
title: The Guns of August
notes: Narrative classic covering the July Crisis to the eve of the Marne. Vivid on personalities; operational detail is dated — cite Herwig or the official histories for numbers and positions.

author: Strachan, Hew
title: The First World War, Volume I: To Arms
notes: Global, thematic; strongest on war plans, mobilization and the strategic context.

author: Zuber, Terence
title: Inventing the Schlieffen Plan: German War Planning 1871–1914
notes: Revisionist: argues the 1905 memorandum was not an operational plan and that 'the Schlieffen Plan' was a post-war construction. Contested — see Mombauer, Holmes, Foley; cite as one side of the debate.

author: Mombauer, Annika
title: Helmuth von Moltke and the Origins of the First World War
notes: Moltke the Younger's planning and conduct in 1914; the principal reply to Zuber on the reality of the plan.

author: Keegan, John
title: The First World War
notes: General history; clear chapters on the war plans and the 1914 campaign.

author: Hastings, Max
title: Catastrophe: Europe Goes to War 1914
notes: 1914 from the July Crisis to the trench line; good on the human scale and the Belgian and Serbian fronts.

author: Reichsarchiv
title: Der Weltkrieg 1914 bis 1918. Die militärischen Operationen zu Lande, Band 1: Die Grenzschlachten im Westen
notes: German official history; volumes 1, 3 and 4 cover the West in 1914. Authoritative for German orders of battle, daily positions and orders; apologetic in tone on command decisions, and it measures the campaign by what the German army did — the Belgian and French sides appear only as resistance met. Band 1, pp. 105–120 ('Die Eroberung der Festung Lüttich') is the account of the Liège operation and the reduction of the twelve forts, and is this pack's citation for when each of them fell: it gives the day and the part of the day — an afternoon, a forenoon, an evening — and not the clock. Page references are to the 1925 first edition, digitised at the URL above. Where a fort-by-fort record at clock resolution is wanted, the works to bring in are Donnell and Zuber (docs/sources.md, 'To add as the content lands'). Beyond the forts, this pack cites it with pages for Emmich's order to advance on Liège 'am 4. August früh' and the composition of the Army of the Meuse (p. 109); the 54th Brigade stepping off from Hermée at 2.30 a.m. on 6 August, the one hour the assault account prints (p. 112); Leman's order sending the 3rd Division away, the movement begun in the afternoon of the 6th, and the garrison of the fortress as about 50,000 men against the 6,000 the Germans assumed (p. 117); the marches of 20 August on the line Brussels–Droogenbosch–Waterloo and the III Reserve Corps taking over the screen against Antwerp (pp. 219, 222); and Gallwitz's report that the northern forts of Namur had fallen (p. 395). For the order of battle it is Anlage 1, 'Das deutsche Westheer am 18. August 1914, beim Beginn des Vormarsches' (pp. 664–687), that this pack cites: it prints every army with its battalion, squadron, battery and gun totals, and under each army every corps with its commander, its chief of staff and its two divisions. pp. 69–70 give what came before it — the deployment areas the Aufmarschanweisungen laid down for each of the seven armies and the four cavalry corps, and the Nordarmee in Schleswig-Holstein; p. 71 records that the transfer of the IX. Armeekorps from the 2. to the 1. Armee was foreseen from the start, which is why the deployment list on p. 69 and the order of battle on pp. 667–668 put that corps in different armies. pp. 688–691 carry the same treatment of the French army, which this pack uses to arbitrate where Edmonds's Appendix 3 and the content disagree. For the routes (sand-23b.6.2) it was read again for its dated situation sketches, which are printed in the text and not in the map pocket: Skizze 2 (p. 195), the 6th and 7th Armies on the morning of 14 August; Skizze 3 (p. 347) and Skizze 7 (p. 506), the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Armies on the mornings of 21 and 25 August; Skizze 8 (p. 538), the 4th and 5th Armies on the morning of 24 August. The narrative behind them: pp. 214–225 the advance of the wheeling wing 18–20 August (20 August 'ein reiner Marschtag', the 1st Army's objectives on the line Brüssel–Droogenbosch–Waterloo and every corps' halting place, the 2nd Army on Mont-St. Jean–La Gatte, the 3rd on Spontin–Celles–Ciergnon); pp. 263–302 the battle in Lorraine corps by corps; pp. 348–430 the Sambre, Namur and Mons; pp. 505–535 the pursuit to 27 August, with the 2nd Army's positions on the evening of the 25th and its objectives for the 26th at pp. 508–509; pp. 537–567 the centre; pp. 568–603 the left wing. **The volume's narrative stops on 27 August** — nothing after that date can be cited to it, which is why the Guise routes were re-pointed to Bd. 3 and the Marne routes keep no pages.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1914, Volume I: Mons, the Retreat to the Seine, the Marne and the Aisne, August–October 1914
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: British official history. Authoritative for the BEF's daily positions and the Le Cateau/Marne/Aisne narrative. The volume was revised twice; where this pack gives a page number for Volume I it cites source:edmonds-1933, the third edition, because that is the edition that is digitised and was read. Page numbers do not carry between the two.

author: Ministère de la Guerre, État-major de l'Armée, Service historique
title: Les Armées françaises dans la Grande Guerre, Tome I, 1er volume: La guerre de mouvement (opérations antérieures au 14 novembre 1914)
notes: French official history with annex volumes of orders (e.g. Instruction générale no 2, the 6 September order of the day). Authoritative for French orders of battle and positions.

author: Wikipedia contributors
title: Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (English)
notes: Used only for uncontested biographical dates (birth, death) pending the citation standard in sand-23b.1. Never cite for operational claims.

author: Pais, Abraham
title: 'Subtle is the Lord…': The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein
notes: The standard scientific biography; relativity 1907–1919, the Entwurf theory, the 1914 eclipse expedition, the counter-manifesto.

author: Crelinsten, Jeffrey
title: Einstein's Jury: The Race to Test Relativity
notes: The astronomers and the eclipse tests 1911–1922, incl. Freundlich's 1914 expedition and internment.

author: Heilbron, J. L.
title: H. G. J. Moseley: The Life and Letters of an English Physicist, 1887–1915
notes: Moseley's law, his enlistment in 1914 and death at Gallipoli.

author: Ungern-Sternberg, Jürgen von; Ungern-Sternberg, Wolfgang von
title: Der Aufruf 'An die Kulturwelt!': Das Manifest der 93 und die Anfänge der Kriegspropaganda im Ersten Weltkrieg
notes: Text, signatories, genesis and aftermath of the Manifesto of the 93.

author: Beesly, Patrick
title: Room 40: British Naval Intelligence 1914–1918
notes: The Admiralty's signals-intelligence section from the 1914 codebook captures to the Zimmermann telegram; the forward link from 1914 wireless.

author: Horne, John; Kramer, Alan
title: German Atrocities, 1914: A History of Denial
notes: The standard study of the August 1914 reprisals in Belgium and France and of the franc-tireur myth; for the Belgian chapter and the historiography notes.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1914, Volume II: Antwerp, La Bassée, Armentières, Messines and Ypres, October–November 1914
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: British official history, second volume; the 1925 first edition, digitised at the URL above. Its narrative begins on 19 September 1914, so it is not a source for the Belgian army in August: the Antwerp chapters cover 19 September to 6 October. What this pack cites it for at page resolution is the two casualty notes to the retrospect — Note I, 'The British Losses' (p. 466), which prints the Adjutant-General's return for 14 October – 30 November and the later unit-by-unit reckoning totalling 58,155, and the grand total from the beginning of the campaign, 3,627 officers and 86,237 other ranks (p. 467); and Note II, 'The German Losses' (pp. 467–468), which prints the figures the Reichsarchiv supplied on request, adding to 134,315, with its own warning that the missing-and-prisoner numbers in them are too high. Also read at page resolution for Flanders: the defences and siege of Antwerp (pp. 32, 35, 47, 62), and the four new German reserve corps of the Fourth Army — their raising and Falkenhayn's reasons for engaging them (pp. 122–123), their transport and detrainment west and south-west of Brussels from 13 October (p. 122), and their divisions in action on 19 October (p. 168). p. 147 dates General d'Urbal's assumption of command of 'Le Detachement d'Armee de Belgique' to 20 October. Read at page resolution for the Flanders routes: p. 62, the capitulation of Antwerp signed at Contich on the evening of 9 October and formally surrendered on the morning of the 10th; p. 64, Kitchener's instruction that Rawlinson cover the Belgian Army's retirement 'from the line Ghent–Selzaete to the area Ostend–Thourout–Dixmude'; p. 69, the decision of 6 October to concentrate the B.E.F. 'in the area Doullens–Arras–St. Pol' and Joffre's intentions of the 7th putting the Second and Tenth Armies under Foch; p. 72, the German attack of 11 October on 'the entire length of the French line from Arras to Vermelles'; p. 103, the Allied dispositions on 15 October, with the Belgian Army 'On Yser. Five divisions from Dixmude to Nieuport' and the French Territorial divisions between Poperinghe and Ypres; p. 122, the transport, detrainment west and south-west of Brussels and westward advance of the four new Reserve corps to the line Courtrai – Thourout by the evening of 18 October; p. 147, General d'Urbal taking command of 'Le Detachement d'Armee de Belgique' on 20 October with his headquarters at Rousbrugge; pp. 168, 170 and 173, the four corps' sectors from 19 to 21 October. Because its narrative begins on 19 September, it is not a source for any path that ends before that date, and twenty-one citations on such paths keep no pages and say so.

author: Tyng, Sewell
title: The Campaign of the Marne 1914
notes: Operational narrative from the interwar official histories; clear on the detached corps — Antwerp, Namur, Maubeuge — and on the Belgian 4th Division's journey round by Le Havre and Ostend.

author: Steg, Jean-Michel
title: Le jour le plus meurtrier de l'histoire de France: 22 août 1914
notes: The reconstruction, from the French Army's own death records, of the roughly 27,000 French soldiers killed on 22 August 1914; the source for the figure and for Rossignol and the Ardennes that day.

author: Spears, Edward L.
title: Liaison 1914: A Narrative of the Great Retreat
notes: Memoir of the British liaison officer at Lanrezac's 5th Army headquarters; the eyewitness account of the Rethel meeting of 17 August and of the 5th Army's retreat. Partisan towards the BEF; check against the official histories.

author: Ludendorff, Erich
title: My War Memories, 1914–1918 (Meine Kriegserinnerungen 1914–1918)
publisher: Hutchinson, London; E. S. Mittler, Berlin
notes: Ludendorff's memoir; the first-hand account of the 14th Brigade's night march into Liège and the surrender of the citadel on 7 August 1914. Self-serving on everything after; reliable for the Liège episode where the Reichsarchiv agrees. The citadel episode of 7 August — the white flags seen from La Chartreuse, the drive to the gate in a commandeered Belgian car, hammering on it, and the surrender of the few hundred Belgians inside — is at pp. 36–37; he gives no clock time for it. Volume II (archive.org item mywarmemories19102lude) carries the German reading of the tank battles: the surprise at Cambrai on 20 November 1917, and the sentence 'August 8th was the black day of the German Army in the history of this war.' Cited without pages, from the archive text.

author: Foch, Ferdinand
title: Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire de la guerre de 1914–1918
notes: Foch's memoirs; for the 9th Army at the marshes of Saint-Gond, 6–10 September 1914 — notably silent on the 'situation excellente, j'attaque' line attributed to him.

author: Gallieni, Joseph
title: Mémoires du général Gallieni: Défense de Paris, 25 août – 11 septembre 1914
notes: Gallieni's own account (he died in 1916; published by his family), with a documents annex printing the Paris orders of 3–9 September (Ordre général no 5 of 4 September, the proclamation of 3 September). Written to assert Gallieni's priority over Joffre in the Marne decision; cite the documents, treat the narrative as one side of that dispute. Also the account of the Paris camp and the 6th Army's attack on the Ourcq, including the requisition of the Paris taxis on 6–7 September 1914. Read at page resolution for three things: the proclamation of 3 September, reproduced in facsimile on the unnumbered plate at p. 65, with the posting of it in the first hour of that morning at p. 63; the requisition of the taxis on 7 September and the move of Trentinian's 7th Division from Gagny and Noisy-le-Sec to Nanteuil-le-Haudouin in the course of the night (pp. 162, 167) — he gives no number of cabs; and the drive to Melun on 4 September (pp. 119–123).

author: Kluck, Alexander von
title: The March on Paris and the Battle of the Marne, 1914
edition: English translation of Der Marsch auf Paris und die Marneschlacht 1914 (Mittler, Berlin, 1920), with notes by the Historical Section (Military Branch) of the Committee of Imperial Defence
notes: First Army commander's memoir, completed February 1918. Prints the OHL directives of 27 August and 4 September, the Bülow–Kluck wireless exchange of 30–31 August and the First Army minute of Hentsch's instructions of 9 September. Self-justifying on the turn inside Paris and on Hentsch; cite for what Kluck's headquarters received and believed, not as fact.

author: Ministère de la Guerre, État-major de l'Armée, Service historique
title: Les Armées françaises dans la Grande Guerre, Tome I, 2e volume: Annexes, 1er volume
notes: The order annexes for 24 August – 5 September 1914: Instruction générale no 2 (annexe no 395, 25 August), Joffre's telegrams and the army orders of the retreat. Authoritative for the French texts; page references are to the printed volume (Gallica scan page = printed page + 14).

author: Ministère des Affaires étrangères de Belgique
title: Correspondance diplomatique relative à la guerre de 1914 (24 juillet – 29 août): the Belgian Grey Book
publisher: Brussels; English translation in Collected Diplomatic Documents relating to the Outbreak of the European War (HMSO, London, 1915)
notes: The Belgian government's published diplomatic file: No. 20 the German note of 2 August (German text and translation), No. 22 the Belgian reply of 3 August, No. 71 the memorandum on the delivery. A belligerent's publication, selected for effect on neutral opinion; the texts themselves are authentic. The BYU transcription carries OCR slips, corrected silently.

author: Le Radical (Paris)
title: Le Radical, 5 août 1914 — 'La réponse de la Belgique', p. 2
notes: Paris daily printing the French text of the Belgian reply as released on 4 August; used for the French wording (checked against Le Rappel and La Gazette de France of the same date, and Poincaré, Comment fut déclarée la guerre de 1914, 1939). Newspaper OCR; a few typographic slips corrected by comparison.

author: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (ed.); Epkenhans, Michael (introduction)
title: Alfred Graf von Schlieffen, Denkschrift 'Krieg gegen Frankreich' [Schlieffen-Plan], Dezember 1905 — Volltext und Faksimile
notes: Full German transcription (with Moltke's marginalia) and facsimile of the Boetticher copy, Bundesarchiv-Militärarchiv N 323/19, with an introduction by Epkenhans summarising the Zuber debate. The text quoted in the Document card.

author: Ehlert, Hans; Epkenhans, Michael; Groß, Gerhard P. (eds)
title: Der Schlieffenplan: Analysen und Dokumente
notes: The post-Zuber collection: essays (Groß, 'There was a Schlieffen Plan') and the edited documents, including the December 1905 memorandum and the later Aufmarschanweisungen. For the historiography panel and the German text.

author: Ritter, Gerhard
title: The Schlieffen Plan: Critique of a Myth
edition: translation of Der Schlieffenplan: Kritik eines Mythos (Munich, 1956)
notes: First publication of the 1905 memorandum and its drafts, with Moltke's comments, from the then-lost-and-recovered files; the English text of the memorandum is at pp. 134–148. Ritter's critique of the plan's feasibility is itself a position in the debate.

author: Van Pul, Paul
title: In Flanders Flooded Fields: Before Ypres There Was Yser
notes: Specialist study of the Yser inundation by a hydraulic engineer: the polder system, the locks of the Ganzepoot at Nieuwpoort, and who opened which sluice on which night. Reconstructs the operation of 21–30 October 1914 from the Belgian engineering and unit records, and argues against the older claim that Foch was the author of the idea; the flooding is his subject, the wider battle only its frame.

author: Unruh, Karl
title: Langemarck: Legende und Wirklichkeit
notes: The detailed demolition of the Langemarck legend: the composition of the four new reserve corps (experienced reservists and Landwehr with a minority of volunteers, not a student army), the absence of the singing from contemporary accounts, and the distance between the fighting of late October and the communiqué of 11 November. Cite for the reality against which the myth is measured.

author: Grawe, Lukas
title: Langemarck Myth
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia article: the text of the OHL communiqué of 11 November 1914, the fighting it actually described (10 November, between Bixschote and Noordschote), the composition of the reserve corps, and the myth's later career. Cite for the communiqué's wording and the myth's construction.

author: Jones, Spencer
title: Ypres, Battles of
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia article on the Ypres battles; for First Ypres gives 19 October – 22 November 1914, the armies engaged, German losses of about 130,000 and Entente losses of about 100,000, and the destruction of the British pre-war army. Cite for the round totals beside Edmonds's exact returns.

author: Clark, Christopher
title: The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914
notes: The leading revisionist account of the July Crisis: decision-makers as sleepwalkers rather than conspirators, with Serbian and Balkan agency given full weight and German war guilt distributed across all the chancelleries. Cite as one position in the origins debate, against Fischer.

author: Fischer, Fritz
title: Germany's Aims in the First World War
edition: translation of Griff nach der Weltmacht (Dusseldorf, 1961)
notes: The book that broke the post-1918 consensus: Germany deliberately courted a continental war in July 1914 in pursuit of world power. The thesis every later account of the crisis argues with; cite as a position, not as settled fact.

author: Albertini, Luigi
title: The Origins of the War of 1914
edition: 3 vols, translated by Isabella M. Massey, 1952-1957
notes: The most detailed narrative reconstruction of the crisis, hour by hour, built on the diplomatic documents and on interviews with surviving participants. Still the standard reference for what was sent, received and understood on each day.

author: Mombauer, Annika
title: The Origins of the First World War: Diplomatic and Military Documents
notes: Scholarly edition of the crisis documents in English translation with commentary, drawn from the national colour books and the post-war editions; useful for checking a text against the archival original and for the editorial history of the collections.

author: Great Britain, Foreign Office
title: Collected Diplomatic Documents Relating to the Outbreak of the European War
notes: The belligerents' own published files - the British Blue Book, the German White Book, the Austro-Hungarian Red Book, the Serbian Blue Book, the Russian Orange Book, the Belgian Grey Book - gathered in one English volume. Each colour book was selected and, in places, edited by its government for effect on neutral opinion; the texts are authentic but the selection is not neutral. Where this pack cites it with pages: the Austro-Hungarian note to Serbia of 23 July, French and English in parallel, at pp. 6–8 — among the British diplomatic correspondence, not in this volume's Red Book section, which prints only the Austro-Hungarian introduction and the Narodna Odbrana annexes; the Serbian reply of 25 July at pp. 32–37; Belgian Grey Book No. 20, the German note to Belgium of 2 August, at pp. 309–311; and Grey Book No. 22, the Belgian reply, at pp. 311–312, headed 'Brussels, August 3, 1914 (7 a.m.)'.

author: Kautsky, Karl; Montgelas, Max; Schucking, Walther
title: Outbreak of the World War: German Documents Collected by Karl Kautsky
edition: English translation of Die Deutschen Dokumente zum Kriegsausbruch (Berlin, 1919)
notes: The German foreign-office files on the crisis, published by the new republic to document the old regime's conduct; the collection in which the 'blank cheque' telegram of 6 July 1914 is document no. 15. Compiled with a political purpose - to show the Kaiser's government at fault - but the texts are the archival ones.

author: Brigham Young University Library
title: The World War I Document Archive
notes: Transcriptions of the published diplomatic collections. Used here for the working text of documents whose authoritative printing is cited alongside it; the transcriptions carry occasional OCR slips, corrected silently against the printed collection.

author: Doughty, Robert A.
title: Pyrrhic Victory: French Strategy and Operations in the Great War
publisher: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge MA
notes: The standard operational history of the French army in the war, written from the AFGG and the GQG archives; the spine for Plan XVII, the Ardennes offensive and Joffre's handling of his army commanders.

author: Greenhalgh, Elizabeth
title: The French Army and the First World War
notes: Armies of the Great War series; cited here for the Colonial Corps' losses at Rossignol on 22 August 1914 (p. 41) and for the state of French doctrine in August.

author: Zuber, Terence
title: The Battle of the Frontiers: Ardennes 1914
notes: The only monograph on the Ardennes encounter battles, built from German regimental histories. Zuber's wider argument about the 'Schlieffen Plan' is contested (see source:zuber-2002 and source:mombauer-2001); his tactical reconstruction of 21–23 August is used here for the shape of the fighting, not for its conclusions.

author: Foley, Robert T. (ed. and trans.)
title: Alfred von Schlieffen's Military Writings
notes: Schlieffen's staff rides, war games and memoranda in translation, with Foley's introduction. Cited for what Schlieffen actually wrote as against what the post-war General Staff said he had planned; one of the principal replies to Zuber.

author: Holmes, Terence M.
title: The Reluctant March on Paris: A Reply to Terence Zuber's 'The Schlieffen Plan Reconsidered'
notes: The opening reply in the War in History exchange that ran from 1999 into the 2010s. Cited for the case that the December 1905 memorandum describes a real operational intention; Zuber's rejoinders are part of the same exchange and the pack presents both sides.

author: Showalter, Dennis E.
title: Tannenberg: Clash of Empires, 1914
edition: first published Archon Books, Hamden CT, 1991
notes: The standard operational account of the East Prussian campaign of August 1914: Gumbinnen, the relief of Prittwitz, the encirclement, and the two corps sent from the West.

author: Stone, Norman
title: The Eastern Front 1914-1917
notes: The Eastern Front as a whole, sceptical of the Tannenberg legend and of the German high command's later account of it; cite for the campaign's shape and for the myth-making.

author: Sumpf, Alban
title: Les taxis de la Marne
publisher: L'Histoire par l'image (Réunion des musées nationaux – Grand Palais; with the French ministries of Culture and of National Education)
notes: A short curated study written around the period photographs of the requisition. Cited for the lower end of the taxi arithmetic — 630 taxis and more than 3,000 men of the 103rd and 104th Infantry, requisitioned by Gallieni on 6 September 1914 — and for the judgement that the trains carried the overwhelming majority of the reinforcements and the taxis were not decisive. It is a public-history site rather than an archival study: use it for the figures it states and for the episode's memory, not for the operational narrative, which comes from the AFGG and Herwig.

author: Bruce, Robert B.
title: Pétain: Verdun to Vichy
notes: A short scholarly biography in the Potomac Military Profiles series. Cited here for the organisation of motor supply at Verdun in 1916 — the Bar-le-Duc–Verdun road divided into six sections with repair shops, refuelling points, a commanding officer and traffic police; the Service automobile and the Bar-le-Duc traffic commission at some 9,000 officers and men with 3,900 vehicles; and the first fortnight's loads of 190,000 men, 22,500 tons of munitions and 2,500 tons of other materiel. Sympathetic to Pétain as a commander, which is the bias to watch on the Verdun chapters; the figures are the ones the French service histories give.

author: Mémorial de Verdun
title: La bataille de Verdun (museum resource page)
publisher: Mémorial de Verdun – Champ de bataille, Fleury-devant-Douaumont
notes: The battlefield museum's own account. Cited only for the traffic figures it states for the Bar-le-Duc–Verdun road: 3,500 lorries, 2,000 cars and 800 ambulances in rotation, a lorry every 14 seconds and one vehicle every 5 seconds at the June–July peak, 90,000 men and 50,000 tonnes a week, and 1,200 territorials shovelling 700,000 tonnes of stone. These are the round figures French commemoration has settled on rather than archival returns, and the card says so; the specific loads come from Bruce.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper
publisher: Annalen der Physik 322 (ser. 4, vol. 17), no. 10, pp. 891–921
notes: The special-relativity paper: received 30 June 1905, published 26 September 1905. Cite for what the paper contains and for its date; contemporary volume numbering is 17, the modern continuous series numbering is 322.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energieinhalt abhängig?
publisher: Annalen der Physik 323 (ser. 4, vol. 18), no. 13, pp. 639–641
notes: Three pages; the mass–energy relation, written as a body radiating energy L losing mass L/c². Cite for what the paper says, not for anything later done with it.

author: Bohr, Niels
title: On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules, Parts I–III
publisher: Philosophical Magazine, ser. 6, vol. 26: pp. 1–25 (no. 151, July), 476–502 (no. 153, September), 857–875 (no. 155, November)
notes: The quantum atom as Bohr first stated it. Cite for the model, the stationary states and the hydrogen spectrum; the three parts are one argument and are cited here as one work.

author: Moseley, Henry G. J.
title: The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements, Parts I and II
publisher: Philosophical Magazine, ser. 6, vol. 26, pp. 1024–1034 (December 1913); vol. 27, pp. 703–713 (April 1914)
notes: Moseley's law and the atomic number, in the two papers that established it. Part II is the one that fixes the gaps at 43, 61, 72 and 75. Cite for the physics and for the papers' dates.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Erklärung der Perihelbewegung des Merkur aus der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie
publisher: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (Berlin), 1915, pp. 831–839
notes: Read 18 November 1915: Mercury's anomalous perihelion advance and the doubled light deflection, on field equations Einstein revised again a week later. Cite for the perihelion result and the date.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation
publisher: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (Berlin), 1915, pp. 844–847
notes: Read 25 November 1915; four pages, the last of the four November papers, and the field equations in their final form. Cite for the equations and the date, not for the priority argument with Hilbert.

author: Corry, Leo; Renn, Jürgen; Stachel, John
title: Belated Decision in the Hilbert-Einstein Priority Dispute
notes: The printer's proofs of Hilbert's paper of 20 November 1915, read as showing that what Hilbert first submitted was not generally covariant and did not contain the explicit field equations. One side of a live argument — Winterberg (2004) and others dispute the reading of the proofs; cite it as a position, not a verdict.

author: Schwarzschild, Karl
title: Über das Gravitationsfeld eines Massenpunktes nach der Einsteinschen Theorie
publisher: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (Berlin), 1916, pp. 189–196
notes: The first exact solution of the field equations, written on the Russian front and presented for the author by Einstein on 13 January 1916. The header carries the presentation date; the paper opens by naming the problem Einstein set in the Mercury paper of 18 November 1915.

author: Schulmann, Robert; Kox, A. J.; Janssen, Michel; Illy, József (eds)
title: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Volume 8: The Berlin Years — Correspondence, 1914–1918
notes: The wartime correspondence. Schwarzschild's letter of 22 December 1915 enclosing his solution is doc. 169; quotations here follow the English supplement translation and are cited as translations.

author: Voigt, Hans-Heinrich (ed.)
title: Karl Schwarzschild: Gesammelte Werke / Collected Works, Volume 1
notes: The collected works, opening with the biographical essay: Schwarzschild's war service (weather station in Belgium, artillery trajectory work in France, then Russia), the pemphigus contracted at the front, the return home in March 1916 and his death on 11 May 1916.

author: Noether, Emmy
title: Invariante Variationsprobleme
publisher: Nachrichten von der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, Mathematisch-Physikalische Klasse, 1918, pp. 235–257
notes: The two Noether theorems. Presented for her by Felix Klein at the session of 26 July 1918, Noether not being a member; dedicated to Klein. Cite for the theorems and the date.

author: Kosmann-Schwarzbach, Yvette
title: The Noether Theorems: Invariance and Conservation Laws in the Twentieth Century
notes: Translation of the 1918 paper with a scholarly history of both theorems and their reception, including the energy-conservation problem in general relativity that Hilbert and Klein set her. The standard modern treatment.

author: Dick, Auguste
title: Emmy Noether 1882–1935
notes: The standard short biography (translated from the 1970 German). Cite for the Göttingen years: the refused habilitation, the courses announced under Hilbert's name, the habilitation of 1919 and the unsalaried years to 1923.

author: Rutherford, Ernest
title: Collision of α Particles with Light Atoms, Parts I–IV
publisher: Philosophical Magazine, ser. 6, vol. 37, no. 222, pp. 537–587; Part IV, 'An anomalous effect in nitrogen', pp. 581–587
notes: The four papers reporting the first artificial disintegration of a nucleus. Cite for what Rutherford observed and concluded in 1919 — not for the reaction as now written, which is Blackett (1925).

author: Blackett, Patrick M. S.
title: The Ejection of Protons from Nitrogen Nuclei, Photographed by the Wilson Method
publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society A 107, pp. 349–360
notes: The cloud-chamber photographs — eight forked tracks in some 400,000 — showing that the alpha particle is absorbed and not scattered, so that the 1919 result is a transmutation of nitrogen into oxygen. Cite for the corrected reading of Rutherford's experiment.

author: Eve, Arthur Stewart
title: Rutherford: Being the Life and Letters of the Rt Hon. Lord Rutherford, O.M.
notes: The letters-and-recollections life by a colleague; the source for most of the well-known Rutherford anecdotes, including the reply about the missed anti-submarine meetings and the 'moonshine' remark of 1933. Cite the anecdotes as anecdotes — Eve rarely dates or stages them precisely, and later tellings vary.

author: Wilson, David
title: Rutherford: Simple Genius
notes: The modern biography. Cite for the wartime work on submarine detection for the Admiralty's Board of Invention and Research, the Manchester nitrogen experiments alongside it, and the move to the Cavendish in 1919.

author: Pais, Abraham
title: Niels Bohr's Times: In Physics, Philosophy, and Polity
notes: The companion volume to Pais's Einstein biography: Bohr's Manchester year, the 1913 trilogy and its reception, and Bohr's later life. Same strength and same bias as Pais on Einstein — a physicist writing about physics, thin on the social setting.

author: Dyson, Frank W.; Eddington, Arthur S.; Davidson, Charles
title: A Determination of the Deflection of Light by the Sun's Gravitational Field, from Observations Made at the Total Eclipse of May 29, 1919
publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 220, pp. 291–333
notes: The expedition report itself: the three plate sets, the reductions, the published deflections and the stated grounds for setting the Sobral astrographic plates aside. Cite for the numbers as published; the argument about whether the rejection was justified is Earman & Glymour, Kennefick and Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody.

author: Earman, John; Glymour, Clark
title: Relativity and Eclipses: The British Eclipse Expeditions of 1919 and Their Predecessors
publisher: Historical Studies in the Physical Sciences 11, no. 1, pp. 49–85
notes: The case that the 1919 announcement outran its data and that the discordant plates were dropped because they disagreed with Einstein. The sceptical side of the argument; cite it as one side.

author: Kennefick, Daniel
title: No Shadow of a Doubt: The 1919 Eclipse That Confirmed Einstein's Theory of Relativity
notes: The reply to Earman & Glymour, developed from Kennefick's 2009 Physics Today article: the astrographic plates were rejected by Dyson on instrumental grounds, and Dyson, not Eddington, made the call. The defending side; cite it as one side.

author: Gilmore, Gerard; Tausch-Pebody, Gudrun
title: The 1919 Eclipse Results That Verified General Relativity and Their Later Detractors: A Story Re-told
publisher: Notes and Records of the Royal Society 76, no. 1, pp. 155–180
notes: A re-examination of the 1919 reductions and of the twentieth-century criticism of them, concluding that the published result stands. The most recent round of the argument; cite alongside Earman & Glymour, not instead of them.

author: Museum of the History of Science, University of Oxford
title: 'Dear Harry…' — Henry Moseley: A Scientist Lost to War
notes: The museum's exhibition and research site, built on Moseley's letters and the family papers it holds. Cite for the circumstances of his death on 10 August 1915 — the 38th Brigade signal section, the Turkish counter-attack on Chunuk Bair, the body never recovered, the name on the Helles Memorial — and for the 1915 Nobel nominations.

author: Haber, L. F.
title: The Poisonous Cloud: Chemical Warfare in the First World War
notes: The standard scholarly account of chemical warfare in the war, and the source everyone else's casualty table comes from: p. 243 gives about 186,000 gas casualties for Britain, 130,000 for France, 107,000 for Germany and 73,000 for the United States. Its verdict is that gas was militarily disappointing and a poor return on the industry it consumed. Ludwig Fritz Haber was Fritz Haber's son and an economic historian; he says so, and the book is markedly unsentimental about his father — the bias to watch is a professional economist's scepticism about the weapon's value, not filial defence.

author: Faith, Thomas I.
title: Gas Warfare
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed survey article. Cited for the sequence of first uses — French tear-gas rifle grenades in August 1914, German irritant shell at Neuve-Chapelle in October 1914 and at Bolimów in January 1915, all ineffective; chlorine at Ypres on 22 April 1915 under Haber's direction; phosgene in December 1915; mustard in July 1917 — and for the four-nation casualty table it reprints from Haber (1986) with the caveat that gas casualty data are inherently inaccurate and that for some nations only generalized estimates exist.

author: Heller, Charles E.
title: Chemical Warfare in World War I: The American Experience, 1917–1918
publisher: Combat Studies Institute, US Army Command and General Staff College, Fort Leavenworth (Leavenworth Papers No. 10)
notes: A staff-college study, open access, with a careful narrative of the first gas attacks before it reaches the American chapters. Cited for the mechanics of 22 April 1915 — the release in the early evening, the two French divisions hit (the 87th Territorial and the 45th Algerian) and the gap of about four miles — and for the first French phosgene shells at Verdun on 22 February 1916. It is a doctrinal study written to draw lessons for the US Army, so its interest is in what worked and why; the operational judgements are conventional.

author: Fitzgerald, Gerard J.
title: Chemical Warfare and Medical Response During World War I
notes: Peer-reviewed and open access; the medical and public-health side of gas warfare. Cited for the high end of the casualty range — more than 1.3 million gas casualties and approximately 90,000 deaths by the armistice — and for the ratio inside it: of about 186,000 British chemical casualties, a death toll of about 2.6 per cent, and of the AEF's gas casualties about 1,500 died. Its judgement is that chemical weapons killed proportionally few soldiers and that a chlorine or phosgene attack produced many casualties but few deaths against troops properly prepared and outfitted. Written from the medical literature rather than the operational archives, and one sentence in it garbles the share of casualties gas caused — take the figures it attributes, not its arithmetic.

author: Kramer, Alan
title: Naval Blockade (of Germany)
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed survey of the blockade and its effects. Cited for the nitrogen figures: BASF producing the annual equivalent of 6,000 tons of nitrogen as ammonium sulphate by July 1914, output raised to 200,000 tons a year under a state guarantee, and German industry supplying 90 per cent of the nitrogen for explosives and 70 per cent of agricultural demand by the end of 1915. Kramer's argument elsewhere in the article is that the blockade's effects on German civilians were severe and are understated in some of the literature — a position to note, though the nitrogen figures are not the contested part.

author: Friedrich, Bretislav; Hoffmann, Dieter
title: Clara Haber, née Immerwahr (1870–1915): Life, Work and Legacy
publisher: Zeitschrift für anorganische und allgemeine Chemie 642(6), 437–448
notes: The scholarly reassessment of Clara Immerwahr, by a Fritz Haber Institute director and a historian of science, published with a companion piece by Eckart Henning ('Freitod in Dahlem (1915)', same issue, 432–436). Cited for the doctorate at Breslau in 1900 and for the historiography of her death: that neither Clara nor Fritz Haber left diaries or correspondence from which her motives could be reconstructed, that no farewell letter survives, and that the reading of her suicide as a protest against chemical weapons rests on later authors — Morris Goran in 1947 and 1967, and Gerit von Leitner's Der Fall Clara Immerwahr (1993) — who give no sources for it. Friedrich and Hoffmann are correcting a myth and press their case hard; the pack states their position as a position and names the popular reading beside it.

author: Erisman, Jan Willem; Sutton, Mark A.; Galloway, James; Klimont, Zbigniew; Winiwarter, Wilfried
title: How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world
notes: The centenary assessment of the Haber–Bosch process, by nitrogen-cycle scientists rather than historians. Cited for the patent date — Haber filed on 13 October 1908 on the 'synthesis of ammonia from its elements' — and for its own summary that a hundred years on 'we live in a world transformed by and highly dependent upon Haber–Bosch nitrogen'. The paper's often-quoted estimate of the share of world population fed by synthetic nitrogen is behind the paywall and is deliberately not quoted here.

author: The Nobel Foundation
title: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1918 — Fritz Haber
notes: The awarding body's own record. Cited only for the prize itself: the Chemistry prize for 1918 to Fritz Haber 'for the synthesis of ammonia from its elements', reserved and awarded in 1919, with the Nobel lecture delivered in June 1920. Reference data, in the same register as the biographical dates rule in docs/sources.md — not a source for anything about the gas programme.

author: Reichsarchiv
title: Der Weltkrieg 1914 bis 1918. Die militärischen Operationen zu Lande, Band 3: Der Marne-Feldzug — Von der Sambre zur Marne
notes: German official history, the volume between the frontier battles and the Marne: the operations of the German western armies from the Sambre to the Marne, roughly 23 August to 4 September 1914. It names, day by day and in its own words, the town each Armee-Oberkommando moved its Hauptquartier to, which is this pack's citation for the German commander tracks over the advance; it also carries the move of the Große Hauptquartier from Koblenz to Luxembourg on the morning of 30 August (p. 190). It also prints in full the German texts of three of this pack's Document cards, which were previously cited to Bd. 1 or Bd. 4 in error: the OHL 'Allgemeine Anweisungen an die 1. bis 7. Armee für den Fortgang der Operationen' of 27 August (pp. 7–9, with the assessment of the enemy on p. 4), the Bülow–Kluck wireless exchange of 30 August from both ends (pp. 137 and 177), and the OHL signal to the First and Second Armies of the evening of 4 September (p. 311), which the volume dates 'in der achten Abendstunde'. Bd. 4, which would carry the battle itself, the Hentsch report and Moltke's tour of 11 September, is not digitised. Apologetic on command decisions, like Bd. 1, and it measures the campaign by what the German army did. Chapter 12, 'Die Vorgänge in Belgien bis zum 7. September' (pp. 327–332), is this pack's citation for the IX. Reservekorps after its release from Schleswig: still on the railway to Tirlemont on 25 August, detraining through Louvain, delayed there by the rising of the 26th, and over the Willebroek canal on 30 August with one brigade left to garrison Brussels. Read at page resolution for the battle of St. Quentin (Guise), which Bd. 1 cannot cover: pp. 145–179 carry it corps by corps — the fight for the Oise crossing at Guise on 28 August and Emmich's X. Corps taking the bridges and the town in the fifth hour of the afternoon (p. 147); the X. Corps' 5 p.m. report and the 1st Army's message that it had forced the Somme at Cléry–St. Christ (p. 151); the X. Reserve Corps west of the Oise on the 29th (p. 153); the VII. Corps' 14th Division over the Somme at Ham (p. 153); the cavalry corps at Libermont and Cugny (p. 159); the X. Corps at Mont d'Origny (p. 161); the Guard Corps at Voulpaix (p. 163); the orders for the 30th (pp. 167–169); and where the whole army went to rest on the evening of the 30th (p. 179). pp. 137–143 carry the 1st Army's left wheel past the battle.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1914, Volume I: Mons, the Retreat to the Seine, the Marne and the Aisne, August–October 1914
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
edition: Third edition, 1933 (reprinted 1937) — a thorough revision of the 1922 first edition against the French and German official histories; its pagination differs from the first edition's
notes: The edition of Edmonds Vol. I that is digitised and was read, and therefore the one this pack cites whenever it gives a page number for the BEF in 1914. It names where GHQ was on most nights of the retreat and prints the GHQ operation orders in its appendices, which is this pack's citation for the GHQ track. Do not carry page numbers between this and source:edmonds-1922. Read at page resolution for the BEF's casualty figures as well as its positions: Mons, 'just over sixteen hundred of all ranks' (p. 91); Le Cateau, 7,812 men and 38 guns (p. 191); the Marne, 1,701 for 6–10 September, corps by corps (p. 363). Read at page resolution for the orders of battle as well: Appendix 1, the British Expeditionary Force (pp. 471–484); Appendix 3, the French armies in August 1914, army by army with each corps's divisions and commander (pp. 488–489); Appendix 5, the Belgian army (p. 492); Appendix 6, the German armies (pp. 493–495); and Appendices 2 and 4, which give the establishments — a British division 18,073 all ranks, the Cavalry Division 9,269 (pp. 486–487). p. 45 prints the seven German army strengths for 17 August 1914 in a footnote, attributed to the German official account; p. 19 gives the Belgian field army as the 117,000 that could actually be mobilized, with each division's peacetime station; p. 282 gives the French Sixth Army's composition and 'some 70,000 men' on 5 September; pp. 49–50 give the BEF's concentration area between Maubeuge and Le Cateau. For the routes (sand-23b.6.2) the appendices matter as much as the narrative: they print Sir John French's operation orders night by night, each with its march table and billeting areas — No. 5 of 1 p.m. 20 August (p. 508), No. 6 of 11.55 p.m. on the 21st (p. 513), the supplementary instruction to the Cavalry Division of 11.35 p.m. on the 21st (p. 514), No. 7 of 8.25 p.m. on the 24th (p. 515), No. 8 of 7.30 p.m. on the 25th (p. 516), the 4th Division's own order of 5 p.m. on the 25th (p. 518), the II. Corps' order of 10.15 p.m. on the 25th (p. 520), No. 9 of 8.30 p.m. on the 27th (p. 521), No. 10 of 11.30 p.m. on the 28th (p. 522), No. 11 of 9 p.m. on the 29th (p. 524), and the order for 6 September (p. 551); the table of appendices that names and dates them is at p. xix. Also read at page resolution: p. 116, Note II, 'The Operations of the French Troops on the British Left between 20th and 24th August'; p. 130, 'Maubeuge was invested by the VII. Corps on the south-east and by the IX. Corps (of the First Army) on the north-west'; p. 246, Sir John French's proposal on 31 August 'to retire "westwards" behind the Seine, to an area just west of Paris'; p. 483, the 19th Infantry Brigade formed at Valenciennes on 22 August 1914; p. 493, the footnote to Appendix 6 that the IX. Reserve Corps 'sacked Louvain, 25th August 1914'.

author: Lanrezac, Charles
title: Le plan de campagne français et le premier mois de la guerre (2 août – 3 septembre 1914)
notes: The French 5th Army commander's own book, published after his relief and written to answer it. Day by day, and it names his own headquarters — Rethel, Chimay, the command post at Philippeville on the day of Charleroi, Sézanne — which is this pack's citation for the 5th Army track. It also gives the hour Joffre reached Sézanne on 3 September to relieve him (p. 276). Self-exculpatory throughout on the retreat from Charleroi and on the BEF; cite for where his headquarters was and what he says he was told, and check the judgements against the official histories.

author: Sumner, Ian
title: The French Army 1914–18
notes: A short uniform-and-organisation reference for the French army of the war: the 1914 dress — capote, képi, madder-red trousers — the pre-war attempts to replace it, and the horizon-blue change of 1914–15. Use it for what the army wore and when the regulations changed. It is a popular series and its colour plates are an artist's reconstructions, not evidence; take garment detail and dates from the text, and take nothing about doctrine or casualties from it at all (Doughty and Greenhalgh are the sources for those).

author: Mollo, Andrew
title: Army Uniforms of World War I: European and United States Armies and Aviation Services
notes: The standard one-volume comparison of what the armies of 1914–18 wore, army by army — German field-grey and the covered Pickelhaube, British khaki service dress, the Belgian greatcoat and shako and the 1915 change to khaki. Use it for cut, colour and the dates of pattern changes across several armies at once, which is exactly what a comparison card needs. Same caution as Sumner: the plates are drawn reconstructions and the book is a uniformology reference, not an operational history.

author: Hogg, Ian V.; Weeks, John
title: Military Small Arms of the 20th Century
notes: A reference catalogue of service small arms: calibre, action, magazine capacity and how each is loaded, for the Lebel, the Berthier, the Gewehr 98, the SMLE and the Belgian Mauser alike. Use it for the mechanical facts a kit card states. Hogg wrote a great deal quickly and the early editions carry the odd slip in service dates; where a date matters, check it against the museum record or an official history.

author: Jones, Spencer
title: From Boer War to World War: Tactical Reform of the British Army, 1902–1914
publisher: University of Oklahoma Press, Norman, OK
notes: The scholarly account of what the British army did with the lessons of South Africa: the musketry regulations, the fifteen-aimed-rounds-a-minute standard, the Short Magazine Lee-Enfield and the training that went with it. This is the source for the BEF's rifle fire at Mons being a policy rather than an anecdote. Sympathetic to the reformers and written to argue that the pre-war army was better than its reputation; read the claims about German misidentification of the fire as machine guns alongside Edmonds and Herwig.

author: Messimy, Adolphe
title: Mes souvenirs
notes: The memoirs of the French war minister who tried twice to get the army out of the red trousers — in 1911–12 and again in June 1914 — and the origin, in most English accounts, of Eugène Étienne's answer to him: 'Le pantalon rouge, c'est la France!' A memoir written twenty-three years after the events by a man defending his own record, and the famous sentence reaches most readers through Tuchman quoting him rather than through a stenographic record: cite it as what Messimy remembered being said, never as a transcript.

author: Armémuseum (Swedish Army Museum), Stockholm
title: Object records on DigitaltMuseum — Gevär m/1898, m/1886 Lebel, Mk III Lee-Enfield (AM.032056), m/1889 Mauser
notes: The catalogue records behind the four rifle photographs in the kit plate set, and the authority for what each object is: the museum's own identification, accession number and photograph. Use it for the identification of the object in the frame and for the licence on the photograph. It is a Swedish collection, so it says nothing about how any of these rifles was used in 1914, and its records do not always distinguish sub-patterns — the Lebel record does not say whether the example carries the 1893 modification, and this pack does not claim it does.

author: Hogg, Ian V.
title: Allied Artillery of World War One
notes: The companion volume to Jäger on the other side of the line: a reference catalogue of French, British, Belgian, Italian, Russian and American guns, gun by gun — calibre, carriage, shell, range and the year each entered service. Use it for the mechanical facts a field-gun card states about the Canon de 75 mle 1897, the Ordnance QF 18-pounder and the Belgian 75 mm mle 1905, and for the recoil system that made all of them quick-firers. Same caution as Hogg and Weeks on small arms: Hogg wrote a great deal quickly and the service dates in his catalogues carry the odd slip, so where a date matters, check it against a museum record or an official history.

author: Jäger, Herbert
title: German Artillery of World War One
notes: The German half of the same reference shelf: the field guns, field howitzers, heavy and super-heavy pieces of 1914–18, with the rebuilds and sub-patterns kept straight — which is what a card needs when the difference between the 7.7 cm FK 96 and the FK 96 neuer Art is the whole point. Use it for the German guns' mechanical facts and dates. It is a technical catalogue, not an operational history: it says what the guns were, not how the artillery was used, which is Strachan's and Herwig's ground.

author: National World War I Museum and Memorial, Kansas City; Imperial War Museum, London; Australian War Memorial, Canberra; Gunfire Artilleriemuseum, Brasschaat
title: Object records and gallery labels behind the four field-gun photographs in the kit plate set
notes: The authority for what object is in each of the four field-gun frames, and for the figures the museums themselves publish about them — including the Imperial War Museum's label for its 18-pounder Mark II, which gives the calibre as 3.3 in (8.4 cm), the weight in action as 2,820 lb (1,279 kg), the range as 6,525 yd (5,966 m), and the gun's own service record. Each record is transcribed on the Wikimedia Commons file page for the photograph and is quoted in the corresponding manifest: File:France 75 mm field gun, Model 1897 - National World War I Museum - Kansas City, MO - DSC07528.JPG; File:British 18-pounder mark II field gun - Imperial War Museum 1.jpg; File:AWM-7,7-cm-Feldkanone-96-nA-3.jpg; File:Canon de 75 mle TR (tir rapide Krupp) Gunfire Museum Brasschaat 13-03-2021 10-58-44.jpg. Unlike the rifle set, these are four institutions and four photographers rather than one museum photographing four objects the same way, and the plate set does not pretend otherwise. Cite it for identification and for museum-published figures, never for how the guns were used.

author: Fuller, J. F. C.
title: Tanks in the Great War, 1914–1918
notes: Written by the man who was GSO1 of the Tank Corps and who drafted the Cambrai plan, and published while he was arguing for an armoured army. It is the fullest contemporary account of the Tank Corps' battles and it reprints the founding papers — Swinton's proposal of October 1914 and his tactical paper of February 1916 among them — which is what it is best used for. It is also a brief for the weapon: Fuller calls Cambrai 'the Valmy of a new epoch in war', and his machine counts are the Tank Corps' own. Cite it for the documents and for the counts it states, beside another account wherever the count matters; do not cite it for whether the weapon was decisive. Read from the archive.org text; the pack's tech cards carry no page numbers.

author: Haig, Douglas; Boraston, J. H. (ed.)
title: Sir Douglas Haig's Despatches (December 1915 – April 1919)
publisher: J. M. Dent, London and Toronto
notes: The despatches as the Commander-in-Chief wrote and published them: the Somme, Cambrai, Amiens and the Hundred Days, with the final despatch of March 1919 in which Haig set out his own reading of the war. Precise on times, frontages, formations and the sequence of an attack, because it was written from the operation orders. It is also self-justification, published in the middle of the argument about his own conduct, and silent or thin wherever the record is against him — read every judgement in it as advocacy. The exception worth citing is the final despatch's insistence that tanks and aircraft 'are incapable of effective independent action', which argues against his own weapons. Read from the archive.org text; the pack's tech cards carry no page numbers.

author: Kennedy, Michael David
title: Tanks and Tank Warfare
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed survey of tank development and use in all the belligerent armies. Cited here for the second count of the first tank action — forty-nine Mark I tanks deployed to France on 15 September 1916 and thirty-one across the German lines — which measures something different from Fuller's forty-nine allotted and thirty-two at the starting-point, and is given beside it. A survey, not an operational history: it is thin on the battles themselves and carries nothing on Amiens.

author: Lloyd, Nicholas
title: Hundred Days Offensive
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed survey of the Allied offensive of August–November 1918. Cited for the Amiens advance of 'up to eight miles' — the outer end of a three-way range this pack gives in full — and for the list in which the tank appears fourth of five: logistical support, artillery dominance, air superiority, tanks 'with mixed success', and infantry tactics. Lloyd's larger argument, that the British army of 1918 had learned a method rather than acquired a weapon, is the position this card takes; it is a position, and not the only one.

author: Lupfer, Timothy T.
title: The Dynamics of Doctrine: The Changes in German Tactical Doctrine During the First World War
publisher: Combat Studies Institute, US Army Command and General Staff College, Fort Leavenworth (Leavenworth Papers No. 4)
notes: Open-access staff-college study of how the German army rewrote its defensive and then its offensive doctrine between 1915 and 1918. Cited for the German side of Cambrai: the British surprise attack of 20 November 1917, the deliberate counter-attack ten days later, the lessons drawn from it that winter, and anti-tank defence becoming 'of particular importance in light of the Cambrai experience'. Like Heller (Leavenworth Papers 10) it is written to draw lessons for the US Army, so its interest is in what worked; its operational judgements are conventional and it is not an archive study of the battle.

author: Faulde, Franz
title: Historische Untersuchungen zur Marneschlacht 1914 (Die Sendung des Oberstleutnants Hentsch)
notes: A doctoral dissertation of 1925 given entirely to the Hentsch mission of 8–10 September 1914 — the one work in this registry whose whole subject is the contested point in 1914:historiography-hentsch-authority. Filed as a study by its form: an independent source-critical monograph, not an official history, though it works almost wholly on the official material. Its value here is that it reads the surviving evidence *as* evidence: it sets Tappen's four reports beside Dommes's recollections and shows the two accounts of Moltke's verbal order borrowing each other's wording between 1917 and 1920, which is why the wording of that order is quoted on the card as a recollection and not as a text. It is also this pack's only readable route to Müller-Loebnitz's Die Sendung des Oberstleutnants Hentsch and to Kuhl's Der Marnefeldzug, both of which Faulde quotes by page; the pack cites Faulde for what Faulde says, and names those works as unread. Partisan in one direction that the reader should know: Faulde argues for Bülow's influence as the centre of the affair and is correspondingly sceptical of Hentsch's own two reports. Pagination: the scan prints only two legible folios, '— 48 —' on leaf 50 and a damaged '— 3[1] —' on leaf 33, both giving a leaf-to-page offset of 2; the Inhaltsangabe's section ranges (Der Auftrag 17–29, Hentsch in Mareuil 39–50, Hentsch auf dem Rückwege 50–52) fall on that offset at four boundaries. Every page cited from it was read on the leaf that offset gives and its quoted phrase grepped back.

author: Stevenson, David
title: 1914–1918: The History of the First World War
notes: The standard one-volume history of the war as a whole, strong on strategy, economics and the way the fronts interacted. Used for the shape of the Western Front year by year and for the collapse of 1918; it supports the line at the resolution of a campaign, not of a map sheet.

author: Foley, Robert T.
title: German Strategy and the Path to Verdun: Erich von Falkenhayn and the Development of Attrition, 1870–1916
notes: Archive-based reconstruction of German strategy to the end of 1916 and the standard corrective to the "bleed France white" account of Verdun. Used for the German offensive on both banks of the Meuse and for where it stopped.

author: Prior, Robin; Wilson, Trevor
title: The Somme
notes: The Somme attack by attack, worked from the operation orders and the war diaries, and severe on the command decisions behind them. Used for the ground gained between 1 July and 18 November 1916 — one side of a live argument about Haig.

author: Prior, Robin; Wilson, Trevor
title: Passchendaele: The Untold Story
notes: Third Ypres phase by phase, including Messines, argued against the campaign having a coherent purpose after August. Used for the dates and the ground; its verdict is one side and is written as such.

author: Harris, J. P.
title: Men, Ideas and Tanks: British Military Thought and Armoured Forces, 1903–1939
notes: The tank from its committees to the interwar arguments, and the corrective to Fuller’s own account of Cambrai. Used for the numbers at Flers-Courcelette and for what the machines could actually do (sand-23b.35).

author: Hammond, Bryn
title: Cambrai 1917: The Myth of the First Great Tank Battle
notes: Cambrai from the war diaries, arguing that the battle was an all-arms operation that the tank has taken the credit for. Used for the first day, the depth reached, and the German counter-attack of 30 November (sand-23b.35).

author: Zabecki, David T.
title: The German 1918 Offensives: A Case Study in the Operational Level of War
notes: The five spring offensives analysed as operations, with the argument that they were tactically brilliant and operationally aimless. Used for the frontages, the depths reached and the shape of the salients Michael, Georgette and Blücher left behind.

author: Sheffield, Gary
title: Forgotten Victory: The First World War — Myths and Realities
notes: The "learning curve" case: that the BEF became an effective all-arms army and won the war in 1918. Used for the Hundred Days; it is one side of the argument about British command and is cited as such.

author: Joffre, Joseph
title: Mémoires du maréchal Joffre (1910–1917)
notes: The French commander-in-chief's own account, in two volumes, published in 1932, the year after his death. Tome 1 — the scan at the URL above — runs from his arrival on the Conseil supérieur de la guerre in 1910 through Plan XVII, the frontier battles, the retreat and the Marne; Tome 2 (gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k208186x) carries 1915 to his removal in 1917. It is here because it is the missing side of two arguments this pack already carries as historiography, and in both of them the only voices in the registry were the men arguing against him: 1914:historiography-lanrezac-removal, where Lanrezac's own book of 1920 supplies every word attributed to Joffre at Sézanne, and 1914:historiography-marne-initiative, where Gallieni's Mémoires of 1920 make the claim against GQG. Both quarrels are about Joffre's record and this is the book written to defend it — cite it for what Joffre said he decided and why, never as fact, and never without the other side beside it. Nothing in the pack rests on it yet, and no page may be written from it until a copy is in hand: like source:afgg-1-2-annexes-1 it is on Gallica, which cannot be opened from CI or from an agent's network. A partial French transcription is at fr.wikisource.org ('Mémoires du maréchal Joffre (1910-1917)', about half formatted, and no substitute for the printed pagination). The English translation is The Personal Memoirs of Joffre, Field Marshal of the French Army, tr. Colonel T. Bentley Mott (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1932); the archive.org copies of it are lending-only, and its pages are its own — they do not carry to Plon.

author: Armée belge, Commandement de l'armée
title: The War of 1914: Military Operations of Belgium in Defence of the Country and to Uphold her Neutrality (L'action de l'armée belge pour la défense du pays et le respect de sa neutralité)
edition: English translation of the report of the Belgian army command for the period 31 July – 31 December 1914, published in French as La guerre de 1914: L'action de l'armée belge pour la défense du pays et le respect de sa neutralité — Rapport du commandement de l'armée (Chapelot, Paris, 1915)
notes: The Belgian army command's own narrative of the 1914 campaign, and the volume that covers the months source:edmonds-1925 does not. Edmonds's second volume opens on 19 September 1914, so it carries neither the field army's withdrawal into the fortified position of Antwerp on 18–20 August nor the sorties of 25–26 August and 9–13 September, which several events and twenty-one route citations in this pack were pointing at it for (sand-23b.22, sand-23b.6.2). This report does: Chapter III, 'Operations in Combination with the Armies of the Guaranteeing Powers, 6th to 20th August', ends with the army inside the entrenched camp of Antwerp on the 20th; Chapter V, the same title for 20 August to 27 September, carries both sorties; Chapter VI is the defence and fall of Antwerp; Chapter VIII is the Yser. Read for what it is. It is short — nine chapters and a set of plates, not an operational history — it was written and published in 1915 while the war was being fought and while Belgium's case against the invasion was being made, and it defends the army's conduct in every line; it gives days and rarely hours, so a time of day taken from it is nominal and must say so. No page number has been written from it yet: the citations that were left empty when Edmonds II was found not to cover them are still empty, and re-pointing them at this volume, page by page, is separate work.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1916, Volume I: Sir Douglas Haig's Command to the 1st July: Battle of the Somme
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: British official history, the first of the two Somme volumes: Haig's assumption of command on 19 December 1915, the winter's preparations, the plan of the offensive, and 1 July 1916 division by division. First of the ten volumes for 1916–18 brought into the registry together (sand-23b.36) so that the Western Front after 1914 can rest on rung 1 of the hierarchy rather than on the studies the front-line layer currently uses — here, source:prior-wilson-2005, which is an argument about Haig as well as an account of the battle. Its appendix volume is a separate book with its own pagination and is not in this registry. Nothing cites this volume yet and no page may be written from it until it is read; the scan above is the Digital Library of India copy, which this repository can open.

author: Miles, Wilfrid
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1916, Volume II: 2nd July 1916 to the End of the Battles of the Somme
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: The Somme from 2 July to 18 November 1916, compiled by Captain Wilfrid Miles rather than by Edmonds, who edited the series. This is the official account of Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, the first action in which tanks were used — which the tech rail presently takes from source:fuller-1920, the Tank Corps' own senior staff officer writing a brief for the weapon, and from source:1914-1918-online-tanks, a survey. An official history is rung 1 and a unit history rung 3; this volume is what should be carrying that count. Nothing cites it yet. Note that the tank numbers for 15 September are disputed between the sources already in the registry, so when this volume is read the count it gives goes beside them rather than over them.

author: Falls, Cyril
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1917, Volume I: The German Retreat to the Hindenburg Line and the Battles of Arras
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: The German withdrawal to the Hindenburg Line in February–March 1917 and the battles of Arras and Vimy that followed, compiled by Captain Cyril Falls. The volume that matters for the shape of the front in 1917: the withdrawal is the largest single change to the line between 1915 and 1918 and the front-line layer draws it from secondary works. The series' 1917 appendix volume is digitised separately (archive.org, in.ernet.dli.2015.210681) and is separately paginated. Nothing cites this volume yet.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1917, Volume II: 7th June – 10th November: Messines and Third Ypres (Passchendaele)
publisher: HMSO, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: Messines and Third Ypres. The one volume of the 1916–18 series with no url in this entry: no openly readable digitisation of it was found, and docs/sources.md forbids writing a link that has not been checked. Until one is in hand the pack keeps source:prior-wilson-1996 for Third Ypres, which is a study and says so. It is also the volume of the series historians argue with rather than simply use — Edmonds compiled it himself, thirty years after the campaign, and its handling of the casualties and of the ground is contested; when it is read, it is read the way rung 1 of the hierarchy says to read an official history, knowing whose army it defends.

author: Miles, Wilfrid
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1917, Volume III: The Battle of Cambrai
publisher: HMSO, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: Cambrai, 20 November – 7 December 1917, compiled by Captain Wilfrid Miles: the massed tank attack of the first morning, the fight for Bourlon Wood, and the German counter-attack of 30 November that took most of the ground back. The pack tells that battle from source:hammond-2008 and, for the German side, source:lupfer-1981, with source:fuller-1920 — written by the officer who drafted the plan — for the Tank Corps' own account. This volume is the official record of all three. Nothing cites it yet.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1918, Volume I: The German March Offensive and its Preliminaries
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: The winter of 1917–18, the extension of the British front southward to take over from the French, and Operation Michael from 21 March 1918 — the deepest German advance since 1914 and the largest single movement of the line the front-line layer has to draw. Presently carried by source:zabecki-2006, a study of the offensives as operations. Nothing cites this volume yet.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1918, Volume II: March–April: Continuation of the German Offensives
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: The end of Michael in front of Amiens and Georgette on the Lys, March and April 1918. The second of the five 1918 volumes; nothing cites it yet.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1918, Volume III: May–July: The German Diversion Offensives and the First Allied Counter-Offensive
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: Blücher on the Chemin des Dames, the Matz, the second battle of the Marne, and the counter-stroke of 18 July 1918 — the turn of the year's fighting, and the point at which the front-line layer's line starts moving east again. Nothing cites this volume yet.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1918, Volume IV: 8th August – 26th September: The Franco-British Offensive
publisher: HMSO, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: Amiens on 8 August 1918 and the advance to the Hindenburg Line. The official account of the day the tech rail describes from source:haig-despatches-1919 — the commander's own despatches, advocacy from end to end — and from source:1914-1918-online-hundred-days, which is where the 'up to eight miles' comes from. Both are the wrong rung for a frontage and a depth. Nothing cites this volume yet.

author: Edmonds, J. E.; Maxwell-Hyslop, R.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1918, Volume V: 26th September – 11th November: The Advance to Victory
publisher: HMSO, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: The breaking of the Hindenburg Line to the armistice. The last volume of the series for France and Belgium, and the one that closes the front-line layer's last snapshot. Its id carries both compilers because Volume IV of the same year is Edmonds alone and the two would otherwise collide. Nothing cites it yet.

author: Toll, Ian W.
title: Pacific Crucible: War at Sea in the Pacific, 1941–1942
notes: First volume of the Pacific War trilogy: Pearl Harbor to Midway. The modern narrative of record in English for the opening year, and unusually good on the Japanese side because it reads the post-war interrogations against the Japanese official history rather than through Fuchida.

author: Toll, Ian W.
title: The Conquering Tide: War in the Pacific Islands, 1942–1944
notes: Second volume: Guadalcanal to the Marianas. Carries the island road and the submarine campaign, and is the volume for Saipan and the civilian catastrophe on it.

author: Toll, Ian W.
title: Twilight of the Gods: War in the Western Pacific, 1944–1945
notes: Third volume: Leyte Gulf to the surrender. The volume for the Philippines, Iwo Jima, Okinawa and the argument the bomb was decided on.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II
notes: The semi-official American naval history, written by a historian commissioned into the Navy with access to the operational records. Authoritative on American movements and losses; partisan on personalities — Morison sat in judgement on Fletcher and on Halsey at Leyte, and later scholarship has revised him on both. Volumes III–XIV cover the Pacific.

author: Parshall, Jonathan; Tully, Anthony
title: Shattered Sword: The Untold Story of the Battle of Midway
notes: Midway rebuilt from the Japanese records — kodōchōsho action reports, the Senshi Sōsho, the ships' own damage narratives. It dismantles the version that came down through Fuchida (the "five fateful minutes", the decks packed with fuelled aircraft) and is the study to cite for anything about Nagumo, Yamaguchi or the Kidō Butai.

author: Frank, Richard B.
title: Guadalcanal: The Definitive Account of the Landmark Battle
notes: The standard operational account of the campaign on land, at sea and in the air, using both American and Japanese records. Cite it for Edson's Ridge, for the naval battles of November 1942 and for Japanese strengths, which pre-1990 American accounts consistently overstate.

author: Robertson, Breanne (ed.)
title: Investigating Iwo: The Flag Raisings in Myth, Memory, and Esprit de Corps
publisher: Marine Corps History Division, Quantico, Virginia
notes: The Marine Corps' own account of how the men in Rosenthal's photograph were identified, misidentified and re-identified, published alongside the 2016 and 2019 board findings. The one source to cite on who is in the picture: it prints the photogrammetric analysis, the official portraits and the Corps' admission that it got two of the six wrong for seventy years.

author: Kakehashi, Kumiko
title: So Sad to Fall in Battle: An Account of War Based on General Tadamichi Kuribayashi's Letters from Iwo Jima
publisher: Presidio Press, New York (trans. Giles Murray; first published in Japanese, 2005)
notes: Built on Kuribayashi's letters home, which it prints at length. Filed as a study rather than as primary because the letters reach the reader through the author's selection and argument; it is the only substantial English window onto the Iwo Jima garrison from the inside.

author: Sledge, Eugene B.
title: With the Old Breed: At Peleliu and Okinawa
notes: A mortarman of K/3/5 writing from notes kept in his pocket Bible. The enlisted account of Peleliu and Okinawa against which the operational histories are read; unsparing, and to be used for what the ground was like rather than for dates and positions.

author: Agawa, Hiroyuki
title: The Reluctant Admiral: Yamamoto and the Imperial Navy
publisher: Kodansha International, Tokyo (trans. John Bester; first published in Japanese as 『山本五十六』, Shinchōsha, 1969)
notes: The standard Japanese life of Yamamoto in English translation, written with access to his letters and to men who served with him. Sympathetic — the title is its thesis — and to be balanced against Toll and Parshall & Tully on the operational judgements.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume III: The Rising Sun in the Pacific, 1931 – April 1942
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: The first of the nine Pacific volumes of Morison's fifteen, and the one that opens where this arc opens: the Manchurian and China incidents, the drift to war, Pearl Harbor, the Philippines, the Malay Barrier and the Java Sea. Read the series note here and take it as attached to all nine. Morison wrote as a serving officer with a commission from Roosevelt and access no outside historian had — he was at sea for much of what he describes — and nothing since matches the coverage: fifteen volumes over an ocean, ship by ship. That closeness is also the limit. He is writing about men he knew, often while they were alive and sometimes for their families, and his judgements have not aged as well as his narrative: source:frank-1990 and source:toll-2015 correct him on Savo Island, where his account of the responsibility for the defeat is now a minority position, and source:parshall-tully-2005 takes apart his Midway, which rests on source:fuchida-okumiya-1955 for the Japanese side. Cite him for what American ships did and when, put a later work beside him for why. The series is still in copyright and in print (the Naval Institute Press and University of Illinois Press reissues); the Internet Archive's own scans are lending copies, and this registry does not link the open user uploads of the Little, Brown printings because their standing is not clear — which is why these nine entries carry no url. The bibliographic detail in them was nevertheless read off the title and copyright pages of those page images rather than taken from a catalogue.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume IV: Coral Sea, Midway and Submarine Actions, May 1942 – August 1942
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
