notes: Coral Sea, Midway, the Aleutians diversion, the first year of the submarine campaign, and the Guadalcanal landings of 7 August 1942. The copyright page of the 1958 printing reads 'Copyright 1949 … Published September 1949'. Its jacket claims the Midway chapters are 'the first to be written from Japanese as well as American sources', and the Japanese sources in question are largely source:fuchida-okumiya-1955: this is the volume source:parshall-tully-2005 was written against, and on the Japanese carriers — what was on their decks, when, and why they were caught — Morison is now known to be wrong. Cite him here for the American side and for the sequence of the American strikes, and cite Shattered Sword for anything happening aboard Nagumo's ships. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume V: The Struggle for Guadalcanal, August 1942 – February 1943
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: The seven naval actions of the Guadalcanal campaign — Savo Island, the Eastern Solomons, Cape Esperance, Santa Cruz, the two nights of the naval battle of Guadalcanal, Tassafaronga and Rennell Island — which ADR 0019 keeps inside one pack rather than splitting into seven. The year is not what the catalogues say. Every catalogue consulted (Open Library, Wikipedia, the standard series lists) dates this volume 1949; the copyright page of the 1958 printing reads 'Copyright 1948 … Published September 1948 … Reprinted October 1948', which cannot be reconciled with a 1949 publication, and the printing history matches source:morison-vol-3's line for line, as two volumes issued together would. The item is followed here over the catalogue, but the conflict is unresolved and anyone with a first printing in hand should settle it. Morison's Savo Island is the part of this volume later work argues with: he wrote close to the event and to the officers involved, and source:frank-1990 and source:toll-2015 reach a different distribution of blame. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume VI: Breaking the Bismarcks Barrier, 22 July 1942 – 1 May 1944
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: The central Solomons and the New Guinea coast: the night actions off New Georgia and Vella Lavella, Empress Augusta Bay, the neutralisation of Rabaul rather than its capture. The naval half of the campaign the Army tells in source:miller-1959 and the Marines in source:shaw-kane-1963; the three are read together. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume VII: Aleutians, Gilberts and Marshalls, June 1942 – April 1944
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: Attu and Kiska, then the opening of the Central Pacific drive: Tarawa and Makin in November 1943 and Kwajalein and Eniwetok in February 1944. Morison's account of Tarawa is the naval one — the tide over the reef, the bombardment that was too short — and it sits beside source:crowl-love-1955 for the Army and source:shaw-nalty-turnbladh-1966 for the Marines, who were the ones on the reef. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume VIII: New Guinea and the Marianas, March 1944 – August 1944
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: Hollandia, the Marianas, and the battle of the Philippine Sea. This volume is where Morison's judgement of Spruance's decision not to run west on the night of 18 June 1944 enters the literature, and it is a contested point rather than a finding: source:toll-2015 and source:spector-1985 set the arguments out. Cite it for the carrier movements and the aircraft losses; write the argument about Spruance as historiography. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume XII: Leyte, June 1944 – January 1945
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: The battle for Leyte Gulf — Palawan Passage, the Sibuyan Sea, Surigao Strait, Samar and Cape Engaño — which ADR 0019 keeps as one Battle inside the Philippines pack because the decoy at Engaño is only legible next to what it drew away from Samar. Morison dedicated the volume to Clifton Sprague, who commanded Taffy 3 off Samar, and his handling of Halsey's decision to go north is advocacy as much as narrative; source:toll-2020 is the corrective to read beside it. The first edition is 1958 and the copyright page says so. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume XIII: The Liberation of the Philippines: Luzon, Mindanao, the Visayas, 1944–1945
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: Lingayen Gulf and the amphibious campaign that followed Leyte, and the first sustained kamikaze attacks on a landing force. Published November 1959 by the copyright page. The Army's account of the same months is source:smith-1963. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morison, Samuel Eliot
title: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, Volume XIV: Victory in the Pacific, 1945
publisher: Little, Brown and Company, Boston (an Atlantic Monthly Press book)
notes: Iwo Jima, Okinawa and the last months: the carrier strikes on the home islands, the kamikaze campaign against the radar pickets off Okinawa, and the surrender. Published October 1960 by the copyright page. This is the naval half of the two operations that put the most pressure on ADR 0007 and ADR 0012, and the casualty figures in it are the ones the casualty layer will have to carry rather than the photographs. See source:morison-vol-3 for the note on the series.

author: Morton, Louis
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Strategy and Command: The First Two Years
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: The theatre volume of the Green Books and the one that carries the argument rather than a campaign: War Plan ORANGE and its abandonment, RAINBOW 5, the Europe-first decision, the division of the Pacific between Nimitz and MacArthur, and Japanese policy from 1931. Chapter II is titled 'Japanese Policy and Strategy, 1931 – July 1941', which makes this the natural spine for the pack that opens at Mukden. First printed 1962, CMH Pub 5-1, LC 61-60001, read off the title page of the Center of Military History facsimile. The official host, history.army.mil, answers 403 to this repository and to CI, the way Gallica does for source:afgg-1-2-annexes-1; the url above is the HyperWar hypertext, which is a transcription rather than a page scan — it marks the printed page numbers, and a page cited from it should be checked against the book before it is written.

author: Morton, Louis
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: The Fall of the Philippines
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: December 1941 to the surrender on Corregidor: Clark Field, the Lingayen and Lamon Bay landings, the withdrawal into Bataan, and the collapse of the supply plan that WPO-3 assumed. First printed 1953, CMH Pub 5-2-1, LC 53-63678, read off the title page of the 1993 CMH facsimile. Morton is unusually direct about American failures for an official historian, and the volume is the standard account of them. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Miller, John, Jr.
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Guadalcanal: The First Offensive
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: The Army's Guadalcanal: the strategic decision of July 1942, the Americal and 25th Divisions' arrival, and the offensive that finished the campaign after the Marines had held the perimeter. The Army half of a campaign the Marine Corps wrote first, and worth citing beside source:hough-ludwig-shaw-1958 for exactly that reason. First printed 1949, CMH Pub 5-3, LC 50-13988, read off the title page of the 1995 CMH facsimile. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Milner, Samuel
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Victory in Papua
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: Milne Bay, Buna and Gona — the other first offensive, running at the same time as Guadalcanal and usually left out of an American telling of it. Wanted precisely because a Pacific arc that goes Guadalcanal-to-Okinawa without Papua is a US Navy arc. First printed 1957, CMH Pub 5-4, LC 56-60001, read off the title page of the 1989 CMH facsimile. The Japanese side of the same fighting is source:bullard-2007, which is a translation of the Senshi Sōsho volumes that cover it. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Miller, John, Jr.
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: CARTWHEEL: The Reduction of Rabaul
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: New Georgia, Bougainville, the Huon Peninsula and Cape Gloucester: the year of converging advances that ended with Rabaul bypassed rather than stormed — the clearest single demonstration of the argument ADR 0019 says the island road carries, that the point was to make the next airfield reachable. Title page: Office of the Chief of Military History, Washington, D.C., 1959; CMH Pub 5-5. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Crowl, Philip A.; Love, Edmund G.
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Seizure of the Gilberts and Marshalls
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: Makin, Tarawa, Kwajalein and Eniwetok — the Army's account of the operations the Marine Corps fought the hardest part of, and the volume in which the amphibious lessons of Tarawa are drawn out for the doctrine. Title page: CMH Publication 5-6, Office of the Chief of Military History, Washington, D.C., 1955. Tarawa is where ADR 0019's warning about the imagery bites first: the newsreel footage mattered because it was unbearable, and the casualty figures here are how that is carried instead. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Crowl, Philip A.
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Campaign in the Marianas
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: Saipan, Tinian and Guam: the islands that put Tokyo inside a B-29's range and so decided the shape of the last year, and the campaign in which the Smith-versus-Smith quarrel between Army and Marine command broke into the open — a contested point to be written as historiography rather than settled. The year here is the one field in this entry not read off the item. The CMH facsimile's title page carries 'First Printed' but the year is illegible in the scan; 1960 is taken from the Library of Congress card number 60-60000 printed beside it and from the CMH catalogue, and the foreword is dated 16 March 1959. CMH Pub 5-7-1. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Smith, Robert Ross
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: The Approach to the Philippines
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: Hollandia, Aitape, Biak, Noemfoor, Sansapor and Morotai — the leaps along the New Guinea coast that carried MacArthur's half of the advance to the edge of the Philippines. First printed 1953, CMH Pub 5-8, LC 53-60474, read off the title page of the 1996 CMH facsimile. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Cannon, M. Hamlin
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Leyte: The Return to the Philippines
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: The Leyte landings and the ground campaign that followed them, which lasted long after the naval battle that gets the name. Cite this for what happened ashore and source:morison-vol-12 for the four engagements at sea. First printed 1954, CMH Pub 5-9-1, LC 53-61979, read off the title page of the 1993 CMH facsimile. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Smith, Robert Ross
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Triumph in the Philippines
publisher: Office of the Chief of Military History, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: Luzon from Lingayen to the end, including the destruction of Manila in February 1945 — a month in which most of the dead were Filipino civilians, and the part of this arc where the casualty layer rather than the photograph has to do the work. First printed 1963, CMH Pub 5-10-1, LC 62-60000, read off the title page of the 1993 CMH facsimile; the author's preface is dated 15 March 1961. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Appleman, Roy E.; Burns, James M.; Gugeler, Russell A.; Stevens, John
title: United States Army in World War II — The War in the Pacific: Okinawa: The Last Battle
publisher: Historical Division, Department of the Army, Washington, D.C.
notes: Okinawa from ICEBERG's planning to the end of organised resistance, written by four historians who were with the forces in the Ryukyus — which is why it is the earliest of the Green Books for the Pacific and the closest to its events. It is also unusually full on the Japanese side, with chapters on the Thirty-Second Army's plan of defence; where that rests on captured documents and prisoner interrogation the derivation should be said, because it is a wartime American reading of Japanese intentions. First printed 1948, CMH Pub 5-11-1, LC 49-45742, read off the title page of the 1993 CMH facsimile. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962.

author: Hough, Frank O.; Ludwig, Verle E.; Shaw, Henry I., Jr.
title: History of U.S. Marine Corps Operations in World War II, Volume I: Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal
publisher: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, Washington, D.C.
notes: The first of the Marine Corps' five volumes: the interwar development of amphibious doctrine and landing craft — the part of the story that explains why any of the later landings were possible — then Wake, the Philippines and Guadalcanal to February 1943. Cite it beside source:miller-1949 rather than instead of it; each service wrote the campaign it fought. The title page carries no year, only Library of Congress card number 58-60002; 1958 is taken from that and from the Internet Archive's record of the volume. Same reachability note as source:morton-1962 — the official Marine Corps host is not openly reachable from here and the url is the HyperWar transcription, whose text carries the printed page numbers.

author: Shaw, Henry I., Jr.; Kane, Douglas T.
title: History of U.S. Marine Corps Operations in World War II, Volume II: Isolation of Rabaul
publisher: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, Washington, D.C.
notes: TOENAILS and New Georgia, the northern Solomons and Cape Torokina, and the New Britain campaign — the Marine half of the year source:miller-1959 tells from the Army's side and source:morison-vol-6 from the sea. Title page: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, 1963. Same reachability note as source:hough-ludwig-shaw-1958.

author: Shaw, Henry I., Jr.; Nalty, Bernard C.; Turnbladh, Edwin T.
title: History of U.S. Marine Corps Operations in World War II, Volume III: Central Pacific Drive
publisher: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, Washington, D.C.
notes: Tarawa, the Marshalls, Saipan, Tinian and Guam: the volume that carries the assault on Betio hour by hour, and the one to cite for what happened on the reef rather than source:morison-vol-7, which is the account from the ships. Title page: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, 1966. Same reachability note as source:hough-ludwig-shaw-1958.

author: Garand, George W.; Strobridge, Truman R.
title: History of U.S. Marine Corps Operations in World War II, Volume IV: Western Pacific Operations
publisher: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, Washington, D.C.
notes: Peleliu and Angaur, the Marines in the Philippines, and Iwo Jima. The Umurbrogol has its own chapters here — 'The Umurbrogol Pocket: 29 September – 15 October' and 'To the Bitter End' — and this is the volume the Peleliu pack rests on, an operation whose necessity is itself contested and should be written as historiography. Title page: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, 1971. Same reachability note as source:hough-ludwig-shaw-1958.

author: Frank, Benis M.; Shaw, Henry I., Jr.
title: History of U.S. Marine Corps Operations in World War II, Volume V: Victory and Occupation
publisher: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, Washington, D.C.
notes: Okinawa from the Marine side — the northern half of the island, then the Shuri line and the drive south — and the occupation of Japan and north China that followed. Note that this Frank is Benis M. Frank, the Marine Corps historian, and is a different person from Richard B. Frank of source:frank-1990; the ids are deliberately dissimilar. Title page: Historical Branch, G-3 Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps, 1968. Same reachability note as source:hough-ludwig-shaw-1958.

author: Bōeichō Bōei Kenshūjo Senshishitsu (War History Office, National Institute for Defense Studies, Japan Defense Agency)
title: Senshi Sōsho (戦史叢書) — War History Series
notes: Japan's official history of the war, and the thing this arc most needs and least has. It is the counterpart of Morison and the Green Books — 102 volumes compiled by the War History Office from the surviving records and from the recollections of the officers who fought — and it is essentially unreachable in English. Only three volumes have been translated: two by the Corts Foundation on the Dutch East Indies, one of which is source:remmelink-2021, and the Papua and New Britain material by the Australian War Memorial as source:bullard-2007. Nothing on Midway, Guadalcanal as a whole, the Marianas, Leyte, Iwo Jima or Okinawa exists in English from this series. Digitisation at NIDS is partial: the url above is the search system, the images are Japanese only, and a limited portion of the series is online. This entry therefore exists mainly so that citations can be honest about what stands behind them. Where the only access is an English-language author quoting a Senshi Sōsho volume, cite that author and say so in the note — never this entry, and never as though the original had been read. source:parshall-tully-2005 is the case where that chain is worth following, because they worked from the Japanese records and say which. Read the series knowing what it is: the surviving record of an army and navy that burned their classified files before the surrender, compiled by the men who had served in them. It has known silences — it does not discuss the use of chemical and biological weapons in China — and its casualty figures differ, sometimes by thousands, from those of Japan's own Ministry of Health and Welfare.

author: Remmelink, Willem (ed. and tr.)
title: The Invasion of the South: Army Air Force Operations, and the Invasion of Northern and Central Sumatra
edition: English translation of extracts from Senshi Sōsho vols 34 and 5; third of the Corts Foundation trilogy, after The Invasion of the Dutch East Indies (2015) and The Operations of the Navy in the Dutch East Indies and the Bay of Bengal (2018)
notes: Filed as official-history because that is its form — it is the Senshi Sōsho, in English — rather than for the use these packs will make of it, which is slight: it covers the southern advance of 1941–42 and Sumatra, at the edge of this arc. It is in the registry for what it demonstrates. It is the only volume of Japan's official history that a reader of this project can open, read and cite in English without a library, being published open access; and one open volume out of 102 is the honest measure of the problem stated in source:senshi-sosho. The publisher's page above is reachable from here; the OAPEN copy of the PDF, which the publisher points to, refuses this repository's requests, so no direct link to the file is given.

author: Bullard, Steven (tr.)
title: Japanese Army Operations in the South Pacific Area: New Britain and Papua Campaigns, 1942–43
edition: English translation of extracts from the Senshi Sōsho volumes covering the South Pacific Area
notes: The Japanese army's own account of Papua, Kokoda, Milne Bay and New Britain, in English — and therefore the single most useful Japanese-side source in this registry for the first year of the island war, because it covers ground the packs will actually stand on. Cite it against source:milner-1957 wherever the two disagree about what the Japanese command intended, which is often. The Australian War Memorial formerly offered the whole translation as a free page-numbered PDF from its Japanese Research Project site; that address now returns 404 and no replacement was found, so the url is the Memorial's catalogue record for the printed book. No page may be written from it until a copy is in hand. Its ISBN is given in secondary listings but was not confirmed against the item and is omitted.

author: Japanese Research Division, Military History Section, Headquarters, Army Forces Far East / U.S. Army Forces Far East
title: Japanese Monographs
publisher: Military History Section, Headquarters, Army Forces Far East, Tokyo
edition: Series of about 187 numbered monographs prepared 1946–1960; cite the individual monograph by number and title in the citation note
notes: The Japanese-side operational record that is actually in English, and the reason this arc need not be written entirely out of American sources. On instructions issued 12 October 1945, former Japanese officers who had held the relevant command and staff appointments wrote up their operations under the supervision of the Demobilization Bureaux; the drafts were translated and rewritten in English by the Japanese Research Division. The series covers what the packs need — Philippines Operations Record (Mono 1), Midway Operations (Mono 93), Okinawa Operations Record (Mono 135), and the Southeast Area and submarine records for the Solomons. Read the series' own warning first, and pass it on in every note that cites one. The introduction says most original orders, plans and unit journals were lost or destroyed, that many important orders, plans and estimates 'have been reconstructed from memory and therefore are not textually identical with the originals', and that they are nevertheless 'believed to be generally accurate and reliable'. That is a document reconstructed from memory by the losing side under the occupying army: cite a monograph for what a Japanese commander said he intended, in the manner of a memoir, and never for the wording of an order. This registry holds the series as one entry, as it does source:byu-wwi-archive; a monograph a pack comes to lean on heavily earns its own entry then.

author: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, General Headquarters
title: Reports of General MacArthur, Volume II, Part I: Japanese Operations in the Southwest Pacific Area
publisher: General Headquarters, Tokyo; facsimile reprint, U.S. Army Center of Military History, Washington, D.C., 1994
notes: The Japanese conduct of the war in MacArthur's theatre, 'compiled from Japanese Demobilization Bureaux records' as the title page says, printed by MacArthur's Tokyo headquarters in 1950 and reissued unaltered by the Center of Military History in 1994 (CMH Pub 13-1, LC 66-60007). Its own foreword is the caveat, and it is a remarkable one for an official publication: MacArthur while he lived refused to allow the Reports to be reproduced because he believed they needed 'further editing and correction of some inaccuracies', and the Department of the Army, publishing them after his death, states that it 'must therefore disclaim any responsibility for their accuracy'. Cite it, quote that disclaimer in the note, and put a modern study beside it. The scan above is open and was read for this entry; the Center of Military History's own copy is behind a host that refuses this repository's requests.

author: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, General Headquarters
title: Reports of General MacArthur, Volume II, Part II: Japanese Operations in the Southwest Pacific Area
publisher: General Headquarters, Tokyo; facsimile reprint, U.S. Army Center of Military History, Washington, D.C., 1994
notes: The second book of the same volume, carrying the later campaigns and the appendices, among them the Japanese navy's order of battle and losses. A separate physical book with its own pagination, which is why it is a separate entry. CMH Pub 13-2; same 1950 printing, same 1994 facsimile, and the same disclaimer of accuracy quoted in source:macarthur-reports-2-1, which is where the note on the series is.

author: League of Nations, Commission of Enquiry
title: Appeal by the Chinese Government: Report of the Commission of Enquiry (the Lytton Report)
edition: Official No. C.663.M.320.1932.VII; signed at Peiping 4 September 1932, circulated 1 October 1932
notes: The document at the centre of the pack that opens this arc. ADR 0019 makes the case for beginning at Mukden on 18 September 1931 because the Pacific war carries the cleanest demonstration of a causal chain the project has: the railway, the conquest, the League's finding, Japan's departure, and nothing done. This is the finding. Chapter IV is 'Narrative of Events in Manchuria on and Subsequent to September 18th, 1931' and Chapter V is Shanghai; the numbering above is the League's own document number, read off the Secretary-General's covering note in the scan. Quote it as a Document with the original wording, in the manner of §7 of docs/sources.md, rather than paraphrasing what the Commission concluded — the wording is the point. The scan above is open and in English.

author: Toll, Ian W.
title: Pacific Crucible: War at Sea in the Pacific, 1941–1942
publisher: W. W. Norton & Company, New York
notes: First of the Pacific War trilogy: Pearl Harbor to Midway, with a long opening on the Japanese naval establishment and its politics that is unusually good on why the war was begun. Toll is the readable modern narrative the arc will lean on for continuity, and he incorporates the post-1990s revisions — source:parshall-tully-2005 among them — that Morison predates. He is a synthesis, not an archive study: for a strength, a time or a position, prefer the official histories and cite Toll for the connective account. Verified against catalogue records only; no ISBN is recorded, and the 2012 date some catalogues give is the paperback.

author: Spector, Ronald H.
title: Eagle Against the Sun: The American War with Japan
notes: The one-volume scholarly history of the American war with Japan, and the best single frame for the arc: strategy, inter-service politics, intelligence and logistics rather than battle narrative, and unsentimental about all of them. Written by a historian who had run the Navy's own history programme, and still the standard survey forty years on. Some catalogues date it 1984; the Free Press hardback recorded in the Internet Archive's cataloguing of the physical book is 1985, which is what is written here. Verified against catalogue records only, not the item; no ISBN is recorded.

author: Dower, John W.
title: War Without Mercy: Race and Power in the Pacific War
notes: The reason this arc cannot be told as a sequence of landings. Dower reads the propaganda, the cartoons, the training material and the private language of both sides and shows a war conducted by each as against a race rather than a state — the American 'exterminationist' rhetoric and the Japanese doctrine of purity together, which is the point: it is not a book about one side's racism. It is what the packs draw on for why prisoners were rarely taken, why surrender was rare, and why the casualty arithmetic of 1945 was argued the way it was. It is an argument and is cited as one, beside the operational sources rather than instead of them. Verified against catalogue records only; no ISBN is recorded.

author: Ienaga, Saburō
title: The Pacific War: World War II and the Japanese, 1931–1945
edition: Translated from Taiheiyō Sensō (Iwanami Shoten, Tokyo, 1968); published in Britain in 1979 by Blackwell as Japan's Last War
notes: A history of the war by a Japanese historian, written in Japan, arguing that it began in 1931 and that it was made possible by what Japanese education and the Japanese state had done to their own people — the case Ienaga spent decades fighting the Ministry of Education in court over. It is in this registry because a Pacific arc whose only Japanese voice is a translated operations record has no Japanese argument in it, and because Ienaga's periodisation is the one ADR 0019 adopts. Polemical, and cited as an argument. Verified against catalogue records only; the New York edition and the 1968 Japanese original are as recorded there, and no ISBN is written here.

author: Evans, David C.; Peattie, Mark R.
title: Kaigun: Strategy, Tactics, and Technology in the Imperial Japanese Navy, 1887–1941
notes: The standard English account of how the Imperial Japanese Navy thought, built and trained before the war: the decisive-battle doctrine, the night-fighting and long-lance torpedo tactics that won Savo Island and the Solomons night actions, and the shipbuilding and aviation programmes behind them. Built on Japanese sources, and the book to cite when a pack has to say why a Japanese force did what it did rather than merely what it did. Verified against catalogue records only; no ISBN is recorded.

author: Peattie, Mark R.
title: Sunburst: The Rise of Japanese Naval Air Power, 1909–1941
notes: The companion to source:evans-peattie-1997 on naval aviation: the carriers, the aircraft, and above all the aircrew training programme, which was superb, tiny, and never replaced — the fact behind the difference between the Japanese carrier force of 1942 and the one of 1944. Cite it for the technical and doctrinal background to Pearl Harbor, Midway and the Philippine Sea. Publisher and year taken from the Internet Archive's cataloguing of the physical book (Annapolis, Naval Institute Press, 2001); no ISBN is recorded.

author: Drea, Edward J.
title: Japan's Imperial Army: Its Rise and Fall, 1853–1945
notes: The army that source:evans-peattie-1997 is for the navy, and the one that matters most at the start of this arc: how a service came to hold that it could act against the policy of its own government, which is what the Kwantung Army did at Mukden in 1931 and what the pack that opens the arc has to explain. Also the frame for the army's conduct of the island campaigns and its refusal of surrender. Verified against catalogue records only; no ISBN is recorded.

author: Hotta, Eri
title: Japan 1941: Countdown to Infamy
notes: The Japanese decision for war, from Japanese sources: the liaison conferences of 1941 and an argument that few of the men in them believed the war could be won and none was willing to be the one to say so. The counterpart on the Japanese side to what source:clark-2012 and source:fischer-1967 are to July 1914 in this registry — a decision-for-war study, to be cited for what the participants said and as one reading of why. Verified against catalogue records only; no ISBN is recorded.

author: Cook, Haruko Taya; Cook, Theodore F.
title: Japan at War: An Oral History
notes: Sixty-odd Japanese people — soldiers, sailors, pilots, nurses, factory workers, colonists, a survivor of the Nanjing garrison, survivors of the firebombing — interviewed in the late 1980s about the war they had lived through. Filed at the memoir rung because that is what it is: testimony given forty-five years after the event, cited for what a person says they saw and believed and never as evidence for a time, a strength or a position. It is here because the sourced vignette is the instrument ADR 0019 says will have to carry what the no-gore rule keeps off the screen, and because a vignette needs a voice. Verified against catalogue records only; no ISBN is recorded.

author: Fuchida, Mitsuo; Okumiya, Masatake
title: Midway: The Battle That Doomed Japan, the Japanese Navy's Story
notes: In the registry as a source to cite against, not from. For fifty years this was the Japanese side of Midway in English — Fuchida had led the Pearl Harbor strike and was aboard Akagi at Midway — and it is where the story of the flight decks packed with fuelled and armed aircraft five minutes from launch comes from, which source:morison-vol-4 and every later English account took up. source:parshall-tully-2005 established from the Japanese records that it is not what happened, and raised the further question of how much of the book Fuchida witnessed at all. Cite it where a pack needs to show the received account and where it came from, always beside Shattered Sword, and never for a fact about the Japanese carriers. Note that its editions are several and their pagination differs: the first English edition is the Naval Institute's of 1955, and the Ballantine paperback of 1958 and the Bluejacket reissue of 2001 are separate books for the purpose of a page number.

author: Hastings, Max
title: Retribution: The Battle for Japan, 1944–45
edition: Published in Britain in 2007 by HarperPress as Nemesis: The Battle for Japan, 1944–45; the two are the same book under different titles and their pagination is not interchangeable
notes: The last year at human scale — the Philippines, the submarine campaign, the firebombing, Okinawa, the atomic bombs and the Soviet entry — told through participants on both sides, in the manner of source:hastings-2013 for 1914. Rule 9 of docs/sources.md applies exactly as it does there: take narrative colour and well-known episodes from it, and take numbers and positions from Morison, the Green Books or the Marine histories. Hastings also passes judgement freely, on Japanese conduct and on Allied commanders alike, and those judgements are cited as his. Verified against the Internet Archive's cataloguing of the physical book (New York, Alfred A. Knopf, 2008), whose record carries the British title as a variant; no ISBN is recorded.
